text: It's almost midnight, and you are starving.
Mustard. Half a lemon. That's dinner, apparently.
Then you spot it: the last of the bread.
What you don't see is the bottom of the loaf.
You don't even look. You're busy watching cat videos.
Bite after bite, all the way to the sofa.
And with every bite, something tiny comes along for the ride.
You flop down and lick your fingers. Life is good.
Your cat sniffs the crumbs, and wants nothing to do with you.
Weird.
The TV goes off. The house goes quiet.
While you sleep, the bread keeps growing.
Seven in the morning. Your hand can't find the alarm. Twice.
Your head feels heavy, like it's full of wet sand.
While you brush your teeth, your reflection is a little late.
You watch the coffee miss the cup. You just watch.
The sun is way too bright today. It almost hurts.
The menu won't hold still. You point at anything.
Leo is talking. Your head keeps sinking.
Dude. You look terrible.
Your finger is tapping. You are not tapping it.
On the walk home, the street starts to tilt. You hold on.
Everything is swimming.
A fever. The internet says you're probably just tired. Okay.
A pill, some water. Your hand won't stop shaking.
Cordyceps is a real fungus.
In the forest, one kind infects ants.
It doesn't bite.
It grows: thin threads called hyphae, spreading through the body like roots through soil.
That night, you can't get comfortable. Something feels wrong.
Morning. There are lines on your neck. Dark, branching lines.
You scrub until it burns. They don't go away.
You've seen this pattern before.
You pull the hood up and zip it to the chin.
Nobody needs to see.
Raw steak has never looked this good. That scares you.
The apple tastes like nothing. Like chewing paper.
Even your cat runs from you now.
Hey, buddy. It's me.
Your own phone doesn't recognise your face.
It's your little sister, Mia. You try to sound normal.
Dinner Sunday? Mom's making soup.
Yeah…
You and Mia, years ago. You remember that day perfectly.
You stand at the window. You don't know for how long. Hours.
Then you blink, and you're outside. Barefoot. In the dark.
You don't remember walking here. Your feet do.
In infected ants, the fungus wraps around the muscles.
The brain? Mostly left alone.
You take back control. For now. And you lock the door twice.
You reach for the bread knife.
Your hand reaches for the steak.
You grab your own wrist. It's like fighting a stranger.
Everything hits the floor. So do you.
Make a fist. Three fingers listen. Two don't.
Inside, you pull with everything you have. It barely moves.
Your arm swings on its own. The mirror cracks.
You try to warn your sister. Your thumb has other plans.
You need a doctor. Your right leg doesn't agree.
Your neighbour waves. You try to wave back. It goes badly.
You stop in the middle of the road, and you don't know why.
Watch it!
A pigeon lands, and your head snaps toward it like a hunter.
Leo. Leo will help. You push the door open.
The smell of people hits you. Warm. Alive. Delicious.
A growl comes out of you. You cover your mouth.
Hey! You okay?
Leo can't see you like this. Nobody can.
You run home before anyone else notices.
You slide down the door. You're shaking.
Then, around noon, the ant climbs a stem, bites a leaf…
and holds on. It never decided to.
You wake up standing in a corner, facing the wall.
The room is wrecked. And you remember every second.
You watched it happen.
You lower the hood, and finally, you see it.
It snaps. Something drifts out. You cough and cough.
Ants, with fungus growing out of their heads. Just like you.
The good news: your body runs at thirty-seven degrees.
Too hot for Cordyceps. In real life.
You write it down, so you won't forget. I am still me.
The news says stay indoors. The orange dots are everywhere.
Officials urge everyone to stay indoors.
People with guns, guarding the bridges. From people like you.
You take the photo. In case you ever forget their faces.
The fridge keeps calling you.
You hold it shut with your whole body.
You leave notes for yourself on every lever.
You build a wall to keep the world out, and to keep you in.
In the dark, your veins glow. You don't feel sleepy at all.
Mia is coming to get you. You type no. Your thumb sends okay.
Day seven. The street is empty.
Someone is knocking.
Hello? Anyone in there?
A stranger, checking every house.
Your nails dig into the windowsill.
Your body wants to go to him.
He pushes. You push back. Please leave. Please.
He marks your door. Now everyone will know.
Others shuffle past. Empty. Nobody home behind their eyes.
One of them looks at you. You wave. It doesn't wave back.
Your cat comes back. It sits with you.
It doesn't run this time.
Then you see them. Mia. Leo. And a stranger with a rifle.
It's Mia! Are you in there?
Your name. She came for you.
You run to the window. But the mouth lever is tangled tight.
You want to say her name. Something else comes out.
The light burns. You flinch away like an animal.
You only meant to move the sofa. Your body throws it.
And there they are. Waiting. Afraid of you.
Your sister steps back. Away from you.
A red dot settles on your head.
Stay back!
Hands up. You surrender. But your fingers curl into claws.
Inside, you hang on the levers with all your weight.
To them, you're just a monster, twitching.
You step forward to explain. It comes out as a lunge.
Don't!
You force your knees down. Look. You're harmless. Please.
Mia hesitates.
Is… is that you?
The photo. You hold it out. Remember? It's me.
She knows. She knows that picture.
And that's when the hunger comes back. Stronger than ever.
It comes from everywhere at once.
You lunge. The photo flies out of your hand.
Leo pulls her back. Inches. Just inches.
You freeze. Two orders at once. Stop. Go.
The photo lands in the grass, face up.
Mia looks at the photo, then at you. Leo pulls her away.
Last warning.
One more step, and he will shoot.
Say something. Anything. Her name. The lever won't move.
You're crying. Your hand is still a claw.
They back away slowly, and they never lower the gun.
This is what they see: a monster.
You stop fighting. You just watch them go.
At the gate, Mia looks back. Just once.
Your body turns around. You didn't tell it to.
Out there, the streets belong to people like you now.
And you're still in here. Watching.
Perhaps the worst part of becoming a zombie isn't losing your humanity.
It's being forced to watch yourself lose it.
